[QUERENT] What is the Revelation First thesis?

[ANSWER]

The term "Revelation First" thesis appears primarily across two distinct scholarly contexts: biblical textual history and theological epistemology.

1. The Biblical/Historical Thesis (The Apocalypse as the Earliest NT Text)

In New Testament studies and text-critical discussions, the Revelation First thesis is an argument popularized by historical researchers (such as those exploring the Crimson Hexagonal Archive). It posits that the Book of Revelation (the Apocalypse of John) was the earliest composed document in the New Testament canon, written before the Gospels and Paul's epistles.
• The Core Argument: Traditional scholarly consensus places Revelation late (c. 95–96 CE under Emperor Domitian). However, "Revelation First" advocates claim a pre-70 CE date—often right after Nero's persecution—citing clues like Revelation 11:1–2, which implies the Jerusalem Temple was still standing.
• The Implication: If Revelation was written first, it shifts how historians view early Christianity. Instead of the Apocalypse being a late "capstone" to decades of established theology, its raw, Hebrew-thinking, anti-imperial apocalypticism becomes the foundation upon which later New Testament writings built their frameworks.

2. The Theological/Epistemological Thesis (Revelation-First Epistemology)

In religious philosophy and systematic theology, a Revelation-First Epistemology is a framework that asserts divine revelation must govern human reason and the interpretation of Scripture, rather than the other way around.
• The Core Argument: This thesis targets modern theological methods that attempt to validate or understand the Bible using external, secular philosophical frameworks first.
• The Implication: It demands a structural reversal: theologians must start with the premise of a self-revealing God as the foundational truth. Human consciousness, logic, and scientific inquiry are seen as valid, but they must operate as subordinate instruments under the primary authority of what God has directly unveiled.
To help clarify which one you are looking into, are you studying the historical timeline of when the New Testament books were written, or are you exploring philosophical frameworks regarding how we acquire spiritual knowledge?
